planting.note: Mount on a large, sturdy board or basket lined with sphagnum moss in bright indirect light in partial shade; Giant staghorn eventually grows very large and heavy, so use a mounting surface and hanging hardware rated for substantial weight from the start.

directions: Mount on a large, sturdy board or hang in a heavy-duty basket in bright indirect light; Giant staghorn fern is an Australian epiphyte closely related to the common staghorn fern but distinguished by its massive size and its shield fronds, which overlap and fold upward around the crown to form a distinctive, cupped, antler-shaped nest rather than lying flat against the mount. Unlike the common staghorn, this species does not produce offset pups, so it can only be propagated from spores, making mature specimens slower to come by and more prized among collectors. Given years of growth, a single plant can eventually reach several feet across and weigh well over a hundred pounds, so choose a permanent mounting location and robust hardware from the outset. Soak or thoroughly water the root mass weekly, allowing it to drain fully between waterings, and never let it sit in standing water.

planting.note: Mount on sphagnum-covered boards or plant in hanging baskets in bright indirect light in partial shade; Java staghorn tolerates slightly drier conditions between waterings than most other staghorn species thanks to its finely divided, silvery, hair-covered fronds.

directions: Mount on sphagnum-covered boards or hang in a basket in bright indirect light; Java staghorn fern is an Indonesian epiphyte prized among collectors for its finely divided, drooping, silvery-gray fertile fronds covered in fine hairs (trichomes) that give the whole plant a soft, frosted appearance quite different from the broader, upright fronds of the common staghorn. Its upright, deeply lobed shield fronds clasp the mounting surface and gradually build up a nest of organic debris that feeds the plant, just as in other Platycerium species. The dense hair covering helps the fronds tolerate brief drying between waterings better than some relatives, but the plant still prefers regular soaking of its root mass followed by thorough drainage rather than constantly soggy conditions. It produces offset pups over time that can be separated and mounted individually once they have their own root system, making it easier to propagate at home than non-offsetting species like Platycerium superbum.
